newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Government finances worsen in July.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Government finances worsen in July.

text.p: The Australian government's finances continued to deteriorate in July, with the rolling-12-month underlying deficit rising to A$12.6 billion from A$10.3 billion in the previous month.

Tuesday's Commonwealth Government Financial Transactions report shows that June's 12-month result, which goes into the history books as the 1995/96 financial year figure, understates the current weakness of the government's finances.
At A$10.3 billion, the June 12-month deficit was higher than the A$9 billion that Treasury had forecast.
But it now appears that it was anomalously low: all recent 12-month results since February have been around A$13 billion except for the one that just happened to represent the financial year.

Canberra Watch has not calculated a trendline for the budget deficit. If one were calculated, it would probably show a deficit above A$12 billion lately, around A$2 billion worse than suggested by the June number that everyone focuses on.

The headline 12-month deficit, for what it's worth, was A$8.7 billion in July, much worse than June's A$5.0 billion and representing a spectacular contrast with the small surplus that the former government predicted in the 1995 budget.

With the budget very much the flavour of the year, Canberra Watch will keep a close eye on the rolling 12-month deficit as a way of monitoring the government's progress on the fiscal tightening announced in the August 20 budget.

By June of next year, according to the budget estimates, the 12-month deficit should fall to A$5.6 billion from July's A$12.6 Billion. So that's A$7 billion in improvement and 11 months in which to achieve it.
Other methods of budget watching are confounded by the enormous seasonality of government finances. The 12-month approach removes seasonality, although not volatility.

Importantly, the analysis is vulnerable to shifts in seasonality. For example, if a big payment that occurred in one month last year shifts to the next month this year, the 12-month number will gyrate before returning to a more settled trajectory.
But the method has much to recommend it, and it rang alarm bells about Treasury's A$9 billion forecast for 1995/96 long before other forms of analysis revealed anything.
